questions.questionHtml:

Birbal was one of the nine jewels in the court of Emperor Akbar, who ruled over a vast and diverse kingdom. Akbar was known for his intelligence and wisdom, and he valued Birbal's counsel greatly. The flowers were in full bloom, and the sweet fragrance filled the air. As they enjoyed the beauty of the garden, Akbar grew curious about the intelligence of the animals that roamed his kingdom."Akbar," he said, "I have always wondered how clever animals are in comparison to humans. If given the opportunity, do you think they could learn and understand our language and rules?"Birbal, with a glint in his eyes, replied, "Your Majesty, it is difficult to predict the extent of their intelligence, but I believe that with enough patience and the right guidance, animals could learn a great deal from us."Intrigued, Akbar decided to test this theory. He commanded his men to bring forth a group of animals, consisting of a monkey, a parrot, a deer, and an elephant. He assigned each animal to one of his four wisest courtiers, including Birbal, and instructed them to teach the animals the ways of human life.Over the next few months, the courtiers worked diligently to train the animals. Each animal showed progress, learning various human behaviors and even some basic communication. The other courtiers were proud of their achievements, but Birbal remained humble, knowing that there was still much to learn.One day, Emperor Akbar called the courtiers and their respective animals to his court. He wanted to see the progress they had made. The monkey performed acrobatics, the parrot recited poetry, the deer gracefully danced, and the elephant painted a beautiful picture with its trunk.Amazed, Akbar praised the courtiers and their animals for their remarkable accomplishments. However, he noticed that Birbal appeared to be in deep thought. Curious, Akbar asked him, "Birbal, you seem lost in thought. What is on your mind?"Birbal replied, "Your Majesty, while we have indeed taught these animals to behave like humans, we must remember that they still possess their innate animal instincts. We must be cautious in our expectations, for their nature is not truly changed."As if to prove his point, a servant accidentally dropped a plate of fruits, startling the animals. In an instant, the monkey scrambled for the fruits, the parrot squawked loudly, the deer darted away, and the elephant trumpeted in alarm. The courtiers were left speechless, realizing the truth in Birbal's words.Emperor Akbar nodded, acknowledging Birbal's wisdom. He understood that while humans could share their knowledge with animals, they must also respect their true nature. From that day forward, Akbar appreciated the wonders of the animal kingdom even more, and he continued to cherish the counsel of his wise and beloved friend, Birbal. Q38. Five years ago, in an emotional farewell at home in New Delhi, Mary Kom won a record sixth World Championships gold. Her nearly two-decade-long career had blazed a path for many to come after her, becoming Indian boxing’s ultimate icon, bringing women’s boxing into relevance. As her career — an unlikely Asian Games swansong notwithstanding — winds down, there was plenty of proof at the World Boxing Championships, at the same venue as Kom’s farewell, that the sport remains in good hands. With four Indian finalists keeping the locals excited till the final day of the world event, India had punched above its weight.Nitu Ghanghas, 22, participating in the 48kg category, the one Kom made her own, won a first Worlds medal by sweeping gold. So did veteran Saweety Boora in the 81kg category. Representing both India and the Northeast region in a similar vein to Kom, Lovlina Borgohain shone brightly in the 75kg category and won the gold. It is, however, the emergence of Nikhat Zareen, who won her second World Championship gold on Sunday, as a world-class boxer that is Indian boxing’s crowning achievement. Zareen’s gold last year was followed by sweeping inspirational takes on her life, but this year it is the mastery of her craft that earned her the plaudits. Zareen is as fierce in the ring as she is articulate off it. Male or female, the Hyderabad boxer is easily the most-recognised boxer in the country now. A woman being a fan favourite in a generally male-dominated sport symbolises the trend of Indian boxing.Men’s boxing may have been in a lull ever since Vijender Singh’s 2008 Olympics bronze, with no improvement in sight. But as preparations for the 2024 Paris Olympics go into full flow this year, at the World Championships, the women have shown that boxing in India is their domain. India has more Olympic medals won by women than by men, at any rate. But it is the consistent flow of smashing headlines that the women garner that has given glowing visibility to women’s boxing in India. It is the assured performances at the top level, without flagging in quality, without going off the boil, that makes women’s boxing dependable as a constant source of inspiration. In Ghanghas and Zareen, in Boora and Borgohain, is the continuing lineage of high standards that Kom set in India with her six World Championships. With her consistent showing, Zareen can be counted upon as a Paris Games medal certainty, the only one besides Neeraj Chopra. The very best is yet to come. Q42. (ii) Men's boxing in India has consistently outperformed women's boxing. (iii) Mary Kom's retirement marked the end of successful women's boxing in India. (iv) Nikhat Zareen has won two World Championship golds.

It is the assured performances at the top level, without flagging in quality, without going off the boil, that makes women’s boxing dependable as a constant source of inspiration.
